rounds.proof_sketch: Grid launch: blocks_per_grid = batch_size = 16, so blockIdx.x ∈ {0,1,...,15}. Original guard: (batch_idx >= 16) → always false. Mutated guard: (batch_idx >= 17) → always false. Both guards never trigger since max(blockIdx.x) = 15 < 16 < 17.
rounds.survival_reason: The kernel is launched with exactly `batch_size` blocks (blocks_per_grid = batch_size = 16), meaning blockIdx.x ranges from 0 to 15 inclusive. The original guard `batch_idx >= batch_size` (i.e., batch_idx >= 16) is defensive code that would only trigger if more blocks than needed were launched—which never happens. The mutated guard `batch_idx >= batch_size + 1` (i.e., batch_idx >= 17) is even more permissive but equally irrelevant since the maximum block index is 15. Both conditions always evaluate to false, so the mutation has zero effect on any execution path. This is confirmed by 112 rounds of differential testing showing bitwise identical outputs.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation only relaxes a boundary guard that was already unreachable. To kill this mutant would require changing the grid launch configuration to launch more blocks than batch_size, but the kernel launch parameters are hardcoded relative to batch_size.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should recognize defensive bounds checks as potentially equivalent when the launch configuration guarantees the check cannot trigger. For kernels with exact block-to-work mappings (1 block per batch element), guards like `batch_idx >= batch_size` are dead code under normal operation and mutations to them should be flagged as likely equivalent.
